- **The API is restricted to secure contexts.** MDN says this feature is available only in secure contexts (HTTPS), in some or all supporting browsers.
- **Localhost is an exception.** One blog post notes that exceptions are made for localhost and file URLs for testing.
- **Browsers treat self-signed HTTPS differently.** A Mozilla bug report says that 'https' includes self-signed certs, which have a different security priority than trusted, end-to-end verified https. In that report, Chrome rejected a service worker over a self-signed certificate while Firefox accepted it.
- **Spec discussion.** A WICG discussion notes that if you're really intending to generate unique IDs, you have no guarantee that the API fulfills this contract in an insecure context.

My inference, not stated in these sources: if you click through a certificate warning and the page loads anyway, the browser may still treat the origin as secure, so `isSecureContext` could be true. Whether it is depends on the browser and on whether the certificate is trusted. Testing in the browser console is the quickest check.

I ran one search. The results don't address the exact "visit this website" prompt, but they cover the underlying cause.

- **iOS Safari rejects untrusted self-signed certs outright.** Unlike desktop browsers, it gives no warning or proceed option. The Kurento docs say iOS Safari is the big exception to the above comment. It will outright reject untrusted self-signed certs, instead of showing a security warning.
- **The fix is to install and trust the root CA on the device.** Kurento recommends generating certs with mkcert and then enabling full trust for the installed root.
- **Safari blocks WebSockets on IP-based or self-signed HTTPS origins.** TSplus says Safari on iOS or macOS refuses the websockets connection when the page is served over HTTPS by IP address or with a self-signed certificate. HTTP is not affected.
- **Your SAN must match the hostname.** The code-server docs say the certificate must have a subject alt name that matches the hostname used to reach it. They also report an undocumented requirement that the cert have basicConstraints=CA:true.
- **Your error is likely a chain-validation failure.** A Turris forum report describes iOS closing a wss connection with OSStatus -9807, which means "Invalid certificate chain".
- **Possible regression on newer iOS.** A Boost user reports a self-signed WSS client that worked on iOS 18.1 but failed on iOS 18.3.1, with no resolution in the results.

Practical takeaways: put a DNS name in the SAN and use it instead of the IP, install and fully trust the CA on the device, and make sure the leaf cert has CA-compliant constraints. The results don't confirm whether a missing IP SAN alone causes the WebSocket failure, so test that directly.

The Apple support article covers the core requirements, but the search didn't surface anything on user-added root CAs.

- **Key sizes and hashing:** Apple's article says RSA keys for server certificates and issuing CAs need at least 2048 bits, and that SHA-2 family signatures are required, with SHA-1 no longer trusted for TLS (All TLS server certificates must comply with these new security requirements... key sizes greater than or equal to 2048 bits. Certificates using RSA key sizes smaller than 2048 bits are no longer trusted for TLS.). The SHA-2 and SHA-1 points appear in the same article's hash algorithm section.
- **Subject Alternative Name:** Apple says the server's DNS name must appear in the SAN extension, and names in CommonName are no longer trusted (the DNS name lives in the Subject Alternative Name extension, and CommonName entries are ignored).
- **Validity period:** For certificates whose NotBefore date is after July 1, 2019, Apple requires an EKU extension with id-kp-serverAuth, and a validity period of 825 days or fewer (certificates issued after July 1, 2019 must contain an ExtendedKeyUsage extension containing the id-kp-serverAuth OID, with a validity period of 825 days or fewer).
- **Failure mode:** Non-compliant connections fail, which can break apps, networking, and Safari page loads (connections to TLS servers violating these requirements will fail).

**Not found:** Nothing in the results addresses whether user-added root CAs are exempt from these rules. The Apple article is the primary source for that, so it should be checked directly. Its URL is support.apple.com/103769 (also listed as HT210176). Note that the 825-day limit is a per-certificate rule, and the results don't confirm any exemptions for user-installed roots.

The search turned up a few relevant leads, though nothing that definitively explains your case.

- **Trust settings can be the fix.** ManageEngine's support article says Safari often doesn't recognize self-signed certificates for WebSocket Secure connections. Its workaround is to view the certificate, click Trust, choose Always Trust, and then save settings. The Self Signed/Third Party certificates configured on the server are not recognized on the Safari browser. You will have to configure the Safari browser to trust/allow secure web socket connections to the Endpoint Central server.
- **The exception may not carry over to WebSocket.** A Cendio bug report notes that Safari doesn't let us use WebSockets by default when using a self-signed certificate. The user must manually approve the certificate, but if a user didn't approve the certificate the error message or log message does not give you any clue to what went wrong.
- **Keychain trust alone may not be enough.** In a 2010 WebKit bug report, a developer found that for both servers they used a self signed certificate, which they also added as a trusted certificate to their keychain, which made no difference.
- **A missing Subject Alternative Name may be the cause.** A WebKit comment from 2016 says the reporter couldn't get Chrome or Safari to accept the self-signed server cert without a SAN. The fix suggested there was to regenerate the certificate with a SAN entry for localhost and 127.0.0.1.

Practical next steps: check that the certificate includes a SAN matching the hostname or IP you connect to, and confirm the WebSocket server uses that same certificate. Then reload the page and approve the certificate prompt again. If it still fails, the search results don't give a reliable answer. Safari's developer console or a packet/TLS trace would be the next place to look.

The search only partly covered the query. It found nothing on Secure cookies with IP-address hosts, so that part is unverified.

- **Same-origin WebSocket handshakes:** Electron's docs say the default Origin header for a WebSocket is the http(s) equivalent of the URL's origin, so the connection is treated as same-origin by the server and by SameSite rules. Defaults to the http(s) equivalent of the WebSocket URL's origin (e.g. connecting to wss://api.example.com sends Origin: https://api.example.com), so that the connection is treated as same-origin by the server and by SameSite cookie rules.
- **Strict cookies on WebSockets in Safari:** A WebKit bug report says Safari 14 and 15 did not send Strict cookies over WebSocket in restored or cache-loaded tabs. It seems to be fixed on Safari 15.1, though the report notes a backport was still justified.
- **Strict cookies on the handshake in Safari:** An Apple developer forum thread reports that Safari did not resend HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies on a second wss connection, while the above setup works fine on Chrome/Firefox.
- **Cross-site behavior:** If the SameSite attribute is "Strict", then the cookie is never sent in cross-site requests. That makes same-origin handshakes the case where Strict cookies should be sent.
- **Security context:** An Include Security post notes that cross-site WebSocket hijacking needs cookie auth with SameSite=None and no Origin validation on the server. It also notes that the ws library for Nodejs and for other common webapp frameworks don't enforce validating the Origin.
- **Secure cookies and IP-address hosts:** Nothing in the results covers this. From general knowledge, not these sources, browsers typically refuse Secure cookies set over plain HTTP, and IP-address hosts usually aren't treated as secure contexts. Verify this before relying on it.

Fette","url":"https://conference.greenbytes.de/tech/specs/rfc6455.html"},{"title":"7 TransportProtocols ToC Previous Next","url":"https://reference.opcfoundation.org/Core/Part6/7.5.2/"},{"title":"www.rfc-editor.org","url":"https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc6455.html"},{"title":"app.semanticdiff.com","url":"https://app.semanticdiff.com/gh/ngxson/llama.cpp/commit/42558acbc4c92055f0c7837bb200dadcadeeaf83"},{"title":"sec websocket protocol","url":"https://http.dev/sec-websocket-protocol"}]

The search turned up useful material on the echo requirement, though nothing on token character rules.

- **Server selection:** RFC 6455 handshake examples show the client offering several subprotocols and the server answering with one selected value (the example offers "chat, superchat" and gets "chat" back). The handshake from the server looks as follows with a single Sec-WebSocket-Protocol line. The client sends a list of supported subprotocols ordered by preference. The server selects one from the list and returns the chosen value in the response header.
- **Echo and failure:** A llama.cpp commit message (a secondary source, not the spec) says that when a client requests a subprotocol, the server must echo it back in the handshake response. It adds that without this, browsers reject the connection. This matches the common bug where a server ignores the header and the browser closes the socket.
- **Missing subprotocol:** A W3C bug thread notes that RFC 6455 is incomplete about subprotocol validation. It lists the failure cases the RFC covers, and says the case where the client offers subprotocols but the server returns none is not covered. The browser-side fix proposed there is that the user agent should fail the connection in that case. So a server that sends no Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header in reply to an offered list can cause the browser to abort.
- **Other context:** A draft nanomsg mapping says that if the server supports the requested protocol it MUST respond with the same Sec-WebSocket-Protocol value sent by the client, and otherwise should fail with close code 1002. This is a draft, not the RFC.

**Not found:** The results did not cover the exact token character rules for Sec-WebSocket-Protocol values under RFC 6455, so I can't confirm those from this search. The RFC copy I saw was a rendering, not the official text, and the rfc-editor errata version is the reference to check.

content.content:
The page defines a secure context for HTTPS pages in these terms:

> "Documents are secure contexts when their resources are delivered over an [HTTPS] connection, or are delivered from a loopback (local) address."

For top-level documents, the test is the URL:

> "Top-level documents provide a secure context when their URL is a [potentially trustworthy URL]."

Under the potentially trustworthy origins section, the relevant condition is:

> "A scheme of `https`, `wss`, or `file`."

The page does not mention certificate errors or self-signed certificates. It doesn't say whether a certificate must be valid, trusted, or issued by a CA for an HTTPS page to count as a secure context. The only criterion it gives is the `https` scheme (or a loopback address).

content.content:
**If the server's response names a subprotocol the client didn't request:** Section 4.1 says the client must fail the connection. Step 6 states that if the response "indicates the use of a subprotocol that was not present in the client's handshake," the client "MUST _Fail the WebSocket Connection_."

**If the response omits Sec-WebSocket-Protocol:** Section 4.1 doesn't require failure. It defines "Subprotocol In Use" as the header's value, or null if the header is absent from the server's handshake. Section 1.3 says clients verify that the server returned one of the values from the handshake, but that is a non-normative overview.

**Token grammar:**

- Section 4.1 (item 10), for the client's header: "The elements that comprise this value MUST be non-empty strings with characters in the range U+0021 to U+007E not including separator characters." It adds that the values "MUST all be unique strings," and the ABNF is "1#token."
- Section 4.3 gives the client-side rule as `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol-Client = 1#token`. The server-side rule is `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol-Server = token`.
- Section 4.2.2 (step 4) says the server's value uses the ABNF "(token)."

You might be connecting to a server that is pretending to be","url":"https://forum.peplink.com/t/the-certificate-for-this-server-is-invalid-you-might-be-connecting-to-a-server-that-is-pretending-to-be/31337/2"}]

The search turned up several sources on this, mostly forum threads and vendor docs.

- **The standard workaround works, usually.** A Peplink forum user says that on iOS you tap "show details" on the error page and then "visit this website," and they confirmed it on the latest iOS at the time (Safari on iDevices lets you accept a self-signed certificate presented by a router. Tap "show details" on the error page, then "visit this website.").
- **It can fail.** An Apple Community thread from January 2026 describes a NAS on iOS 26 where the Show Details button did nothing (the button could be tapped but nothing happened). A Jamf user reported a similar dead end with no way to continue or trust the certificate (a "This connection is not private" page with no way to continue anyway or trust the cert).
- **Suggested fixes from that Apple thread.** Check the certificate's hostname, and if Show Details still fails, remove VPN and security add-on apps and force-restart the iPhone (Check the hostname used in the self-signed certificate. If Show Details / Visit this Website isn't working, remove VPN and security add-in apps and force-restart the iPhone.).
- **Safari loops and HSTS.** A Safari 15 developer thread describes the visit-anyway flow looping back to the same error, and an older Jeff Geerling post explains that stale HSTS cache entries can block the exception. His workarounds were a private browsing window or clearing the HSTS cache, which is a Mac-specific procedure (Method 1 is a private browsing session; Method 2 clears the HSTS cache). Those were macOS-era steps, so treat them as a hint rather than a verified iOS fix.
- **Vendor guidance.** Sennheiser's documentation says the warning is expected on local devices because they cannot get publicly trusted certificates, and that the connection is still encrypted (Local network devices cannot obtain and maintain publicly trusted certificates, so they use a self-signed certificate.). Its Safari steps are Show Details, then Visit this website, then confirm the OS permission dialog.

I found no official Apple documentation on this. The most reliable fix I found is to make sure the certificate's hostname or IP matches the address you're using, then retry the Show Details path. If that fails, try a private window or the restart steps above.

The search turned up the long-running WebKit bug that matches your description, though not any recent status update.

- **Core issue (WebKit bug 41419):** Filed in 2010, it reports that secure `wss://` WebSocket connections failed in Safari to a server using a self-signed certificate, even after the certificate was added to the keychain. The reporter found that setting Safari to always trust the certificate made the connection work. We should log the reason when a secure wss WebSocket connection could not be established is the bug's title, and the maintainer agreed that logging the failure was the right first step. He was wary of a bypass warning dialog for WebSocket, since that equals to having no security at all.
- **The "accept on the HTTPS page first" workaround:** A 2011 mailing-list thread describes this exact flow. Accepting the warning on the https:// page in iOS Safari did not carry over to a wss:// connection to "appliance.example.com" is initiated. As issue 41419 states, this will fail in Safari and WebKit. Chrome treats that acceptance as valid for both protocols. A WebKit developer replied that This isn't a WebKit issue. It's an issue for the embedding application.
- **Certificate details:** A later WebKit bug (158345) says that Chrome or Safari would not accept a self-signed server certificate without a Subject Alternative Name, so the cert needs a SAN entry for localhost or 127.0.0.1.
- **Related workaround:** A 2018 comment in bug 158345 suggests that NSURLSession WebSocket is a viable workaround for this issue, and that a fuller fix would mean reimplementing WebSockets on NSURLSessionStreamTask, which is a large change with high regression risk.

I could not confirm whether bug 41419 is still open or fixed in current Safari. Its Bugzilla page shows status NEW, and the search turned up nothing newer. Check the bug page and recent WebKit release notes before relying on either the workaround or a fix.

Search results point to a conflict. Apple's documentation appears to exempt user-added roots from the 398-day rule, but several reports say the 825-day limit still applies to privately trusted CAs on iOS.

- **Apple's exemption:** Apple's 398-day page says "This change will not affect certificates issued from user-added or administrator-added Root CAs." That exemption is quoted from the 398-day change, not the 825-day requirement.
- **Apple engineer comment:** An Apple DTS engineer's post says the 825-day requirement applies to a server certificate issued from one of the Root CAs contained on Apple platforms. The post notes the user-added exemption but does not say whether it covers the 825-day rule.
- **Contrary user report:** A developer forum poster says they experimentally verified that the limit documented here of 825 days is now quietly being enforced for internal Root CAs. In their test, an 826-day certificate failed with a validity error. This is anecdotal and not confirmed by Apple.
- **Unclear definition:** Commenters in another Apple forum thread asked what defines "user-added or administrator-added Root CAs". One reply says the shorter period only affects certificates created with a root that already exists in the trust store of the device.
- **Other browsers:** A Microsoft statement quoted in that thread says certificates that are rooted to a private PKI CA ("locally-trusted anchor") are not limited this way. That is about Edge and Chrome, not iOS.
- **Practitioner report:** An unverified practitioner post describes iOS and macOS rejecting server certificates valid for more than 825 days even when the issuing CA is trusted. A separate Univention thread reports that reducing the validity to 824 days fixed trust, but only after the root was deployed via MDM.

Bottom line: the documentation suggests user-added roots are exempt from the 398-day limit, but the 825-day limit's treatment of user-added roots on iOS is unresolved. The anecdotal reports suggest it may still apply. I didn't find a definitive Apple statement on the 825-day rule for user-added roots. Apple's current support pages (HT210176 and HT211025) would be the place to confirm.

The search didn't turn up a Safari-specific answer about local network permission. The most relevant material is Apple's developer documentation and a few vendor and forum pages.

- **Apple's rule for .local names:** Apple's TN3179 technote says a local DNS name is one ending in `.local`, and all Bonjour operations, including resolving a Bonjour service, require local network access. It applies to the dnssd APIs and to any API built on them. A local DNS name is one ending with `.local` (or `.local.`), per RFC 6762. All Bonjour operations require local network access. This is about native app APIs, not Safari itself, so I couldn't confirm how Safari's own prompt behaves.
- **An unexpected trigger:** An Apple Developer Forums thread reports that `processInfo.hostName` on iOS 18.5 needed the local network permission. An Apple DTS engineer said the technote's wording had missed this case and asked for a bug report. At the time he wrote TN3179 he assumed that the call obviously fell into the resolving a local DNS name category.
- **Vendor claims about unicast fallback (less reliable):** SonicWall and Trend Micro say that .local names often fail over VPNs or with internal DNS. SonicWall says Apple systems send `.local` queries to mDNS rather than unicast DNS, and that two-label names like `corp.local` get forwarded to unicast DNS as well. Trend Micro says iOS devices often can't reach `.local` domains. Neither is an Apple source, and the SonicWall "two-label" claim isn't confirmed by Apple in these results.
- **Apple's older guidance:** Apple's archived support articles recommend suffixes like `.internal`, `.lan`, `.intranet`, or `.private` instead of `.local` for private networks.

If you need Safari's exact behavior, the next step would be to test on a device or look for an Apple document covering Safari and the local network prompt.

content.content:
**Secure**
> "Indicates that the cookie is sent to the server only when a request is made with the `https:` scheme (except on localhost), and therefore, is more resistant to manipulator in the middle (MITM) attacks."

> "Insecure sites (`http:`) cannot set cookies with the `Secure` attribute. The `https:` requirements are ignored when the `Secure` attribute is set by localhost."

**SameSite=Strict**
> "Send the cookie only for requests originating from the same site that set the cookie."

**HttpOnly**
> "Forbids JavaScript from accessing the cookie, for example, through the `Document.cookie` property. Note that a cookie that has been created with `HttpOnly` will still be sent with JavaScript-initiated requests, for example, when calling `XMLHttpRequest.send()` or `fetch()`. This mitigates attacks against cross-site scripting (XSS)."

**`__Host-` prefix rules**
> "Cookies with names starting with `__Host-` must be set with the `Secure` attribute by a secure page (HTTPS). In addition, they must not have a `Domain` attribute specified, and the `Path` attribute must be set to `/`. This guarantees that such cookies are only sent to the host that set them, and not to any other host on the domain."

In short, a `__Host-` cookie needs `Secure`, `Path=/`, and no `Domain` attribute. For example:

```http
// Accepted when sent from HTTPS
Set-Cookie: __Host-ID=123; Secure; Path=/

// Rejected: missing Path=/
Set-Cookie: __Host-id=1; Secure

// Rejected: sets a Domain
Set-Cookie: __Host-id=1; Secure; Path=/; Domain=example.com
```

The search turned up good support for the server-side origin check, but no MDN page.

- **Server responsibility:** A Cobalt guide says the server is responsible for checking the Origin header on the initial handshake, and that a server which skips this check may accept connections from any origin (Cobalt's pentesting guide, citing the same point as a Medium pentesting guide).
- **OWASP's position:** The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (v4.2) describes the same risk, noting that a server that doesn't validate the origin may accept connections from any origin, which can enable CSRF-like attacks. The results suggest that a self-signed certificate for an IP address without a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) entry triggers this error in Chrome, but they don't settle whether the proceed option still appears in current versions.

- **Cause:** Chrome 58 and later check only the SAN field when matching a hostname or IP, ignoring the Common Name. Several sources describe this, including a [Palo Alto Networks knowledge-base article](https://live.paloaltonetworks.com/t5/expedition-articles/access-expedition-gui-using-google-chrome/ta-p/318360) and [TrueNAS community posts](https://www.truenas.com/community/goto/post?id=392791).
- **Bypass:** The sources disagree. The Palo Alto article says a certificate missing the proper SAN gives no option to proceed, so it recommends reissuing the certificate. A [NethServer forum user](https://community.nethserver.org/t/chrome-58-doesnt-work-with-nethserver/6730) reported that the "Advanced → Proceed (unsafe)" exception still worked with a self-signed certificate, though that user's certificate did include a wildcard SAN entry.
- **Fix:** The usual remedy is to regenerate the certificate with the IP address in the SAN field (for example, an `IP.1` entry in the OpenSSL config). The [Graylog community thread](https://community.graylog.org/t/graylog2-https-error-on-chrome/2936) shows this approach being tried.

All of these sources are from about 2017 or later and none tests current Chrome, so the bypass behaviour in recent versions is unverified. A search on the current Chrome release notes or Chromium's certificate error handling would be needed to confirm it.

**Short answer:** The bug is still open (status NEW, unassigned, last comment July 2021), and no fix date has been given. The thread doesn't directly answer whether a self-signed certificate accepted through a browser warning works for WebSocket.

- **Self-signed cert via warning:** Not addressed directly. The thread concerns client certificates, and one commenter notes that a normal page load must come first, with the certificate accepted in the UI, before WebSocket requests work.
- **SAN requirement:** One commenter reports that Chrome and Safari would not accept a self-signed server cert without a SAN, and shows a config that adds one. The thread doesn't confirm whether SAN is required specifically for WebSocket.
- **Fix status:** Alex Christensen said a proper fix would mean reimplementing WebSockets on `NSURLSessionStreamTask`, which carries high regression risk. Youenn Fablet later said work was underway to use the NSURLSession WebSocket API, available as an experimental feature in Safari.
- **Known issues with the workaround:** One user found it worked only once per browser start, failing after a refresh. Another reported per-message deflate problems in Big Sur and iOS 14 betas.

6. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769 (fetched). The page says nothing about user-added roots. The current certificate has no SAN, no explicit EKU and a year-4096 `not_after` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:102-110`, per the investigation). It meets none of the three. Query: "Apple support TLS server certificates requirements iOS 13 macOS 10.15 825 days subjectAltName user-added root CA not affected".

In that bug, the connection worked only after Safari was set to always trust the certificate, and WebKit declined to add a bypass for WebSocket on the grounds that the spec requires failing when verification fails. 8. Each item says what to build to, favourable or not.

1. **Does iOS Safari give the owner a way past this certificate, and does a click-through cover `wss://`?** Tried: the queries under Settled 7, plus "Safari iOS self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address 'visit this website' proceed WebSocket wss fetch exception" and "iOS Safari 'This Connection Is Not Private' 'Show Details' 'visit this website'". 3. **Does a click-through page count as a secure context, and does it keep `Secure` cookies and `SameSite`?** Tried: "self-signed certificate accepted browser secure context crypto.randomUUID certificate error isSecureContext true", "Chrome certificate error proceed unsafe page isSecureContext service worker...". 4. **Does Safari send a `SameSite=Strict` cookie on a same-origin `new WebSocket()`?** Tried: the Settled 2 query. An Apple forum thread (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/104488) reports Safari not resending an HttpOnly/Secure/Strict cookie on a second `wss` connection; WebKit bug 232666 says Strict cookies were missing over WebSocket in restored tabs in Safari 14 and 15, "seems fixed in 15.1". Plan for the header form to be accepted in both cases (it is also what the native clients' bearer path maps to).
5. **Does `history.replaceState` remove the query from Safari's stored history, tab list and iCloud tab sync?** Tried: "history.replaceState remove query string from browser history entry URL sensitive token Safari history records initial URL". 3. **After the owner accepts the warning, does the browser still trust it after closing the tab, after a relaunch, and after the host's IP changes?** I found no source. Favourable: the click-through is a once-per-address step. Unfavourable: the owner sees the warning on each launch; the dialog says so. The plan includes that sentence either way.

The plan should echo the chosen value, which is correct under both readings.
2. A cookie with `Secure` is sent only on `https:` requests. `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from script but still sends it on `fetch`. `SameSite=Strict` sends it only on same-site requests. A `__Host-` cookie needs `Secure`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`. Evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie (fetched). Queries: "SameSite=Strict cookie sent WebSocket handshake same-origin; Secure cookie IP address host".
3. Cookies are scoped by host, not port. The `__Host-` prefix does not narrow that. It only forbids `Domain`, so a cookie reaches every port of the host. This is the same MDN page as line 2.
4. A WebSocket handshake carries `Origin`, and the server must validate it. The protocol does not check it, so a cookie-authenticated socket without an Origin check is open to cross-site hijacking. Evidence: https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/v42/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/11-Client-side_Testing/10-Testing_WebSockets (OWASP, via search result). Query: "WebSocket Origin header not enforced server must validate cross-site WebSocket hijacking...". Header-token auth (a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value) is not sent automatically by the browser, so it is not exposed to this attack.
5. A secure context is defined by the URL scheme (`https`, `wss`, `file`, or loopback). MDN does not mention certificate errors. Evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Secure_Contexts (fetched). For `crypto.randomUUID`, the plan may use it on an https page, but behaviour after a click-through is not stated by the standard. Service workers are known to be refused by Chrome on certificate errors (https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1162772), so the plan must not use one. A fallback for the op id (random bytes from `crypto.getRandomValues`, formatted as a UUID) removes the dependency. See Unresolved 3 for the unsettled part.
6. Apple's rule for trusted TLS server certificates (certificates issued after 1 July 2019): the DNS name must be in the subjectAltName (CommonName is ignored), EKU `serverAuth` is required, validity at most 825 days. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769 (fetched). The page says nothing about user-added roots. The current certificate has no SAN, no explicit EKU and a year-4096 `not_after` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:102-110`, per the investigation). It meets none of the three. Query: "Apple support TLS server certificates requirements iOS 13 macOS 10.15 825 days subjectAltName user-added root CA not affected".
7. WebKit has an open bug since 2010 (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419, status NEW, last modified 2026-01-12) that `wss://` to a self-signed server fails. In that bug, the connection worked only after Safari was set to always trust the certificate, and WebKit declined to add a bypass for WebSocket on the grounds that the spec requires failing when verification fails. A second open bug (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345, status NEW, last comment July 2021) records that a normal page load must come first with the certificate accepted, and that a fuller fix would move WebSocket onto `NSURLSession`; an experimental feature for that exists. Both bugs are open with agreeing reports, which settles that the behaviour exists and is unfixed. It does not tell us what current iOS does, see Unresolved 1. Queries: "Safari WebSocket wss self-signed certificate fails even after accepting certificate exception"; "WebKit WebSocket wss does not use certificate exception accepted in Safari self-signed...".
8. Apple's `.local` rule: all Bonjour operations, including resolving a `.local` name, need local network access in native apps (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3179-understanding-local-network-privacy). That is about native APIs. It does not tell us what Safari does with a `.local` URL, see Unresolved 6.

## Unresolved

Each item says what to build to, favourable or not.

1. **Does iOS Safari give the owner a way past this certificate, and does a click-through cover `wss://`?** Tried: the queries under Settled 7, plus "Safari iOS self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address 'visit this website' proceed WebSocket wss fetch exception" and "iOS Safari 'This Connection Is Not Private' 'Show Details' 'visit this website'". Findings: forum posts describe "Show Details, visit this website" working on a router certificate, but also failing on iOS 26 (Apple Community thread, January 2026). Kurento's docs say iOS Safari rejects untrusted self-signed certificates with no way to proceed (https://doc-kurento.readthedocs.io/en/stable/knowledge/selfsigned_certs.html). Those are not primary sources and they disagree. The WebKit bugs are old and do not cover iOS 26. No vendor text covers the SAN-less IP case. **Build to:** if the click-through covers `fetch` and `wss`, the plan adds nothing. If it does not (the likelier reading of the two open bugs), the plan must still (a) issue a certificate with a SAN for the address, EKU `serverAuth` and validity of 825 days or less, over the same key so the SPKI pin holds, and (b) make the page work without a WebSocket: poll `/api/v1/` with a revision-based refetch, and treat the socket as an upgrade. The acceptance line "moves to the top without a reload" is then met by polling.
2. **Does Chrome, Firefox or macOS Safari let the user proceed past a SAN-less certificate on an IP?** Tried: "Chrome self-signed certificate IP address without subjectAltName IP ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID proceed unsafe still available". Chrome ignores CommonName (since 58, per several vendor KB articles); the sources disagree on whether "Proceed" is then offered, and none test a current release. **Build to:** the same certificate as line 1(a), with the IP in the SAN, so the name error does not arise. A bypass is not needed on this path.
3. **Does a click-through page count as a secure context, and does it keep `Secure` cookies and `SameSite`?** Tried: "self-signed certificate accepted browser secure context crypto.randomUUID certificate error isSecureContext true", "Chrome certificate error proceed unsafe page isSecureContext service worker...". The standard keys on the scheme; no source tests a bypassed page. **Build to:** feature-detect. Make the op id with `getRandomValues` (no `randomUUID` dependency). If cookies are the token transport, the plan needs the Bearer/subprotocol path as the fallback the page uses when the cookie is not stored, so the plan cannot rest on cookies alone.
4. **Does Safari send a `SameSite=Strict` cookie on a same-origin `new WebSocket()`?** Tried: the Settled 2 query. An Apple forum thread (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/104488) reports Safari not resending an HttpOnly/Secure/Strict cookie on a second `wss` connection; WebKit bug 232666 says Strict cookies were missing over WebSocket in restored tabs in Safari 14 and 15, "seems fixed in 15.1". These are reports, not a vendor statement for current iOS. **Build to:** favourable, the cookie works; unfavourable, the page sends the token as a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value (the host echoes it, per Settled 1). Plan for the header form to be accepted in both cases (it is also what the native clients' bearer path maps to).
5. **Does `history.replaceState` remove the query from Safari's stored history, tab list and iCloud tab sync?** Tried: "history.replaceState remove query string from browser history entry URL sensitive token Safari history records initial URL". Found only patterns; one source says replaceState "doesn't prevent the creation of a new entry in the global browser history". The HTML standard says it rewrites the current entry, but no source covers when a browser records the first URL. The code is in the QR URL, so the first navigation records it before any script runs. **Build to:** make the code single-use and short-lived (the pairing window already closes after five minutes or three wrong codes, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). A code that stays in history is then harmless once the window closes or the code is spent. The plan must state that in the spec rather than claim the history is clean.
6. **Does a `.local` name resolve from iOS Safari?** Tried: "Safari iOS .local mDNS hostname Bonjour resolves in Safari browser https local network permission". Only native-API sources. **Build to:** the IP as the URL host (what `local_address()` returns today). If the owner later confirms `.local` works, it can be an additional address; nothing in the plan waits on it.
7. **How many parallel connections Safari opens per host, and how long it keeps them.** Tried none beyond the above; not searched for separately. **Build to:** the pool of 4 must not be the page's budget. Serve the page's files with `Connection: close`, or have the page's total unauthenticated requests before pairing be few (one HTML file with inline-free CSS and JS is three requests). The plan can add a test with 6 parallel requests in `tests/remote.rs` following `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients` (`:3226`).
8. **Does an 825-day limit apply to a certificate under a user-trusted root or a directly trusted self-signed certificate on iOS?** Tried: "Apple 825 days limit applies to user-installed trusted root CA certificates iOS exempt". Apple's page is silent (Settled 6). The 398-day page says user-added roots are exempt, and one forum poster reports the 825-day limit enforced anyway. **Build to:** at most 825 days of validity either way, and the plan names the reissue as part of the address-change story.

## For the owner

Each needs a device. The plan cannot wait on them, and the branch given works in both cases.

1. **On an iPhone, with the current certificate: can the owner proceed past the warning, does the page load, do `fetch` and `new WebSocket` both work afterwards?** Favourable: no certificate work is required for iOS, only for Chrome (Unresolved 2). Unfavourable: the SAN certificate and the polling fallback (Unresolved 1). The plan builds the SAN certificate and the polling fallback regardless, so both outcomes work.
2. **Does the same hold after the SAN certificate is installed (same key)?** Favourable: the socket works. Unfavourable: the page polls. Same build as above.
3. **After the owner accepts the warning, does the browser still trust it after closing the tab, after a relaunch, and after the host's IP changes?** I found no source. Favourable: the click-through is a once-per-address step. Unfavourable: the owner sees the warning on each launch; the dialog says so. The plan includes that sentence either way.
4. **Does the QR code, scanned with the iOS camera, appear in Safari history or iCloud tabs after the page loads?** Favourable: nothing extra. Unfavourable: the code in history is spent or expired by then (Unresolved 5). The plan makes the code single-use in both cases.

I've written the facts file, and `git status` is empty. I ran no spike, because every open browser question needs a real iPhone or iPad. I didn't count the words, so the 1,500-word limit is unchecked.

**Settled from the tree**
- The Stop hook's `last_message` exists only on the hook event (`src/ports/events.rs:24`). No record or `SessionView` field holds it, so a card excerpt on the wire needs a new field.
- Adding request fields touches one construction site. `RemoteReply` is built at about 30 sites, so response headers want a constructor or a `Default`.

**Settled from outside the tree**
- RFC 6455 says a browser fails a socket whose response names a subprotocol it didn't offer. Base64url is allowed in an offered value.
- `HttpOnly` cookies are still sent on `fetch`, and a cookie reaches every port of its host.
- Cookie auth on a socket needs an `Origin` check.
- Apple's trusted-certificate rules need a subjectAltName (SAN), the `serverAuth` extended key usage (EKU) and at most 825 days' validity. The current certificate has none of the three.
- Two WebKit bugs from 2010 and 2016 are still open. They report that `wss://` to a self-signed server fails after a click-through, and they predate current iOS.

**Unresolved**
Each item carries its queries and the line the plan must build to.
- Whether iOS Safari lets the owner past the warning, and whether the click-through covers `wss://`. The plan must build the SAN certificate over the same key and a polling fallback either way.
- Whether Chrome offers a bypass for a SAN-less IP certificate. Building the SAN certificate makes this moot.
- Whether a click-through page counts as a secure context. The plan must use `getRandomValues` for the op id.
- Whether Safari sends a `SameSite=Strict` cookie on a WebSocket. The plan must accept the subprotocol token form in both cases.
- Whether `history.replaceState` clears the code from Safari's history. The plan must make the code short-lived and say so in the spec.
- Whether Safari resolves `.local`, and how many connections it opens per host. The plan should use the IP and keep the page to few unauthenticated requests.
- Whether the 825-day limit applies under a user-trusted root. I found no Apple statement, so the plan should stay under 825 days.

**For the owner**
Four device checks, each with a branch that works either way.
